title: Nuclear fission and fusion (physics only)

meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Nuclear fission and fusion (physics only), specification section 4.4.4.
final_note: You worked through Nuclear fission and fusion (physics only) — 8 specification statements.

concepts.def: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, for example a uranium or a plutonium nucleus, into two smaller nuclei. It is a nuclear change, not a chemical one: the nucleus itself breaks apart.
Fission happens to nuclei that are both large and unstable. Uranium and plutonium are the examples the specification gives. A small nucleus, or a large but stable one, does not undergo fission.

Fission that occurs without the nucleus being made to split by anything arriving from outside. Spontaneous fission is rare, so a sample of fissionable fuel left alone does not split apart of its own accord to any appreciable extent.
Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. The neutron is taken into the nucleus rather than bouncing off it, and the nucleus then splits.

The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Both are much smaller than the original nucleus, but neither is a tiny fragment: this is not like alpha decay, where a small particle leaves a nucleus that is almost unchanged.
As well as the two smaller nuclei, a fission emits two or three neutrons. These are free neutrons travelling away from the site of the fission, and they are what makes a chain reaction possible.
A fission also emits gamma rays. These are electromagnetic radiation, emitted along with the two smaller nuclei and the two or three neutrons.
Energy is released by the fission reaction. The energy is not produced by burning the fuel chemically; it is released when the nucleus itself splits.

concepts.term: Kinetic energy of the fission products
concepts.def: All of the fission products have kinetic energy. The two smaller nuclei and every neutron emitted move away from the fission, so each of them carries kinetic energy, not just the neutrons.

The neutrons released by one fission may go on to be absorbed by other unstable nuclei, causing those nuclei to split and release neutrons of their own. Because each fission can release two or three neutrons, the number of fissions can grow from one generation to the next.
In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled. Controlling it does not mean stopping it: it means holding the rate of fission steady so that the energy released by the reactor is controlled.

A chain reaction in which the number of fissions grows unchecked. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction, so a very large amount of energy is released in a very short time.

In a diagram of fission, a small circle arriving at a large nucleus represents the neutron being absorbed. The large nucleus is then shown splitting into two smaller circles of roughly equal size, with two or three further small circles (neutrons) leaving, and gamma rays shown as wavy arrows.

A chain reaction diagram is drawn in generations. One fission at the top releases neutrons; each neutron that is absorbed by another nucleus produces a further fission in the next row. If every neutron drawn causes a fission, the number of fissions per row multiplies from one row to the next.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. Fusion is the opposite kind of change from fission: fission splits one large nucleus, fusion joins two light ones.

concepts.term: Mass converted into the energy of radiation
concepts.def: In fusion, some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation. The heavier nucleus that forms therefore has slightly less mass than the two light nuclei that joined together.

options: The joining of two light nuclei together to form a single heavier nucleus.
The breaking up of a nucleus into all of its separate protons and neutrons.
The splitting of a small and stable nucleus, such as a carbon nucleus.
The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as a uranium nucleus.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.

mcqs.q: An engineer needs a fuel whose nuclei can undergo fission. Which choice is suitable, and for the right reason?
options: Helium, because its nucleus is very small and very stable.
Hydrogen, because its nucleus is the lightest of them all.
Plutonium, because its nucleus is large and unstable.
Lead, because its nucleus is large and does not decay.
mcqs.explain: Plutonium is one of the two examples the specification gives, and it meets both conditions: the nucleus is large and it is unstable.

mcqs.q: Usually, for fission to occur, what must happen to the unstable nucleus first?
options: It must be hit hard by a fast-moving electron.
Nothing: it will shortly split all on its own.
It must absorb a gamma ray from another atom.
It must first absorb a neutron that hits it.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.

mcqs.q: A sealed sample of uranium is stored on a shelf. Over many years only a very small number of its nuclei split. Why?
options: Fission is happening constantly, but far too slowly to detect.
Uranium nuclei are stable, so they can never undergo fission.
Neutrons cannot be absorbed unless the sample is heated first.
Spontaneous fission is rare, so almost no nuclei split unaided.
mcqs.explain: Fission usually requires the nucleus to absorb a neutron first; without that, only the rare spontaneous fissions occur.

mcqs.q: As well as two smaller nuclei, what does a fission reaction emit?
options: Two or three neutrons, plus gamma rays.
Two or three neutrons, and nothing else.
One neutron only, plus alpha particles.
Two or three protons, plus gamma rays.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the nucleus emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.

mcqs.q: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. What is true of the two nuclei produced?
options: One is almost as large as uranium and the other is very small.
They are roughly equal in size, and both smaller than uranium.
They are always exactly identical to each other in every way.
They are each larger than uranium, since two nuclei formed.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

mcqs.q: Immediately after a fission, in what forms is the released energy carried away?
options: As gamma rays only; the products themselves are left at rest.
As kinetic energy of the two or three emitted neutrons alone.
As kinetic energy of the fission products and as gamma rays.
As chemical energy given out as the uranium fuel burns away.
mcqs.explain: All of the fission products have kinetic energy, and gamma rays are emitted, so the energy released is carried away in both forms.

mcqs.q: Which of the products of a fission reaction have kinetic energy?
options: Only the neutrons, because only they are moving off.
Only the two smaller nuclei, not the emitted neutrons.
Only the lighter of the two nuclei that are produced.
All of them: both nuclei and every neutron emitted.
mcqs.explain: The specification states plainly that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes how a chain reaction gets going?
options: Neutrons released by one fission are absorbed by other nuclei.
Gamma rays released by one fission split the nuclei around it.
Electrons knocked off the atoms go on to split other nuclei.
Heat released by one fission makes the nearby nuclei split.
mcqs.explain: The neutrons emitted may go on to start a chain reaction, because absorbing a neutron is what makes another nucleus undergo fission.

mcqs.q: The specification says the neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. Why 'may' rather than 'will'?
options: Some neutrons escape or are absorbed without causing a fission.
Each neutron does cause a fission, but only after a long delay.
Only one neutron is ever released, so the reaction cannot spread.
Neutrons cause fission only if a gamma ray is emitted as well.
mcqs.explain: A chain reaction only continues if emitted neutrons are absorbed by other unstable nuclei; neutrons that escape the fuel do not, which is what makes control possible.

mcqs.q: In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled. What is the purpose of controlling it?
options: To stop the chain reaction from happening at all.
To stop the fuel from emitting any gamma rays.
To control the energy released by the reaction.
To make the fuel split into equal-sized nuclei.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released.

mcqs.q: What is the essential difference between a nuclear reactor and a nuclear weapon?
options: A weapon uses a fuel a reactor cannot use at all.
In a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled.
In a reactor the chain reaction is stopped entirely.
In a weapon each single fission releases more energy.
mcqs.explain: The specification attributes the explosion caused by a nuclear weapon to an uncontrolled chain reaction, in contrast with the controlled reaction in a reactor.

mcqs.q: A diagram of fission shows a large labelled circle for a uranium nucleus, with a small circle arriving at it from the left. What does the small circle represent?
options: An electron being fired at the nucleus.
A neutron being absorbed by the nucleus.
A light nucleus about to fuse with it.
A gamma ray heading into the nucleus.
mcqs.explain: Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron, and that absorption is what the incoming small circle shows.

mcqs.q: In a chain reaction diagram, one fission at the top releases two neutrons, and each neutron is absorbed and causes a further fission. How many fissions are shown in the third row?
options: 2 fissions
8 fissions
4 fissions
3 fissions
mcqs.explain: Row 1 has 1 fission, which releases 2 neutrons and so gives 2 fissions in row 2; those release 4 neutrons, giving 4 fissions in row 3.

options: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
The joining of two heavy nuclei to form a lighter nucleus.
The splitting of one heavy nucleus into two lighter ones.
The joining of two atoms so that their electrons combine.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of nuclear fusion.

mcqs.q: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. How does the mass of the new nucleus compare with the total mass of the two light nuclei?
options: Exactly the same: mass can never be lost or gained in any change.
Slightly less: some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
Slightly more, because energy had to be supplied to force them together.
Slightly less, because a neutron is given off as the nuclei join up.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the new nucleus is slightly less massive.
